Definition: from G4862 and G5342 (including its alternate); to bear together (contribute), i.e. (literally) to collect, or (figuratively) to conduce; especially (neuter participle as a noun) advantage:--be better for, bring together, be expedient (for), be good, (be) profit(-able for).
BiblicalUsage: Jesus says it is profitable for you that one of your members should perish rather than your whole body be cast into hell, and Caiaphas says it is expedient for us that one man should die for the people. The same word measures profit two ways: Jesus counts the cost of sin against eternity, and Caiaphas counts the cost of one man's life against the nation's safety. Paul picks the word up for the church: all things are lawful, but all things are not expedient, and what is expedient is what builds up.
TheologicalSignificance: My position is that true profit is measured by what lasts, not by what is convenient, and I hold that the cross settles the question: what Christ did was expedient for us in the deepest sense. I take Paul's rule as my own: lawful is not enough, and I want what is profitable for others and for the gospel.
